frozenConceptEvidence.sequence: Source/interest and actual course evidence examined before course scheduling and decision implementation. Closest material animal-biology/ecology response first; physiological and ecology/enterprise candidates challenged sequentially, then implemented. No quota or personal interests invented.
concepts: Combine animal diversity, evolution, ecology and comparative neurobiology with cellular biology, metabolism, physiology, immunity and evidence about disease. Use farming, life-cycle assessment, ethics and sustainability governance to examine animal welfare and animal–environment relationships. Human biomedical study contributes shared mechanisms without replacing species-specific husbandry.

Investigate the cellular, biochemical, physiological and immune mechanisms relevant to animal functioning and health. Retain evolution, ecology and comparative neurobiology while deepening human anatomy, pathology, pharmacology, laboratory work, quantitative analysis and research synthesis. Species-specific nutrition, breeding and veterinary practice remain outside this programme.

Investigate animal populations and the environmental consequences of farming and aquaculture using biodiversity, evolution, ecology, marine biology, sustainable farming and life-cycle assessment. Combine ethics and governance with economics, enterprise, marketing and market research to assess management and innovation; this is not training in animal-feed manufacture or food processing.

courses.name: Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine
courses.contribution: Cellular organisation, biomolecules, enzymes, energy metabolism, heredity and gene expression provide shared biological mechanisms underlying animal functioning. Scientific-paper analysis is actual work; farm-species handling and physiology practicals are not promised.

evidenceFields.description2: Introduces biochemistry, macromolecules, cells, organ systems, DNA and cell function. Connects fundamentals to health and disease and serves as a starting point for medicine, biomedical science, life science or public health; no lab experience needed.
evidenceFields.profile: Introduces the molecular and cellular foundations of life and biomedical science. Students study biological molecules, cells and membranes, communication, enzymes and energy metabolism, cell division, DNA and heredity, gene expression, genomes and biotechnology. Scientific experiments and papers are analyzed through short teaching contributions and a research-based mini-symposium. A responsive final component selects additional life- and biomedical-science topics with the class.
evidenceFields.topics: Biological molecules and chemistry of life; Cells, organelles and membranes; Cellular communication; Enzymes and energy metabolism; Cell cycle and division; DNA and heredity; Gene mutation and molecular medicine; Gene-expression regulation and epigenetics; Genomes; Recombinant DNA and biotechnology
evidenceFields.methods: Scientific-literature searching and synthesis; Analysis of published biological experiments

courses.name: Introduction to Biodiversity
courses.contribution: Actual animal invertebrate/vertebrate diversity, phylogeny, organism identification and microscopy place animals in the tree of life. Broad biodiversity is not a specialist vertebrate-dissection or domestic-animal production course.

evidenceFields.description2: The biosphere consists of millions of living species. In this course we will travel through the tree of life, starting with bacteria and single-celled eukaryotes such as reef-building dinoflagellates and disease-causing apicomplexans. Next, we will look at the multicellular groups: plants, seaweeds, fungi and animals. We will also investigate the relevance of biodiversity for human society in fields such as food and food security, economy, climate and health.
evidenceFields.profile: Surveys the diversity and evolutionary relationships of living organisms across the tree of life. Students examine prokaryotes, protists, fungi, plants and animals, their distinguishing characteristics and ecological roles. Practical work introduces microscopy, organism identification and biodiversity measurement. A small project investigates a selected phylogenetic branch, supported by literature searching, data collection and analysis.
evidenceFields.topics: Biodiversity and its measurement; Phylogenetic relationships; Viruses; Bacteria and archaea; Protists; Fungi; Plant diversity; Invertebrates; Vertebrates and primates; Evolutionary history; Organismal ecological roles
evidenceFields.methods: Microscopy; Organism identification using identification apps; Rank-abundance diagrams; Species-saturation curves; Biodiversity indices; Phylogenetic research; Scholarly database searching; Biodiversity data collection and analysis

courses.name: Introduction to Programming
courses.contribution: Structured Python programming, collections, recursion, testing and debugging provide concrete research-computing tools for reproducible biological/ecological work; animal-specific data or software is not guaranteed.

evidenceFields.description2: Introduces programming and computer science. Covers structured programming, data constructs, testing, debugging and object‑oriented programming with Python, and develops computational problem‑solving skills.
evidenceFields.profile: Introduces computational problem-solving and programming in Python. Students develop structured programs using branching, iteration, functions and data collections, then progress to recursion, exception handling and object-oriented programming with inheritance. Elements of logic, sets and enumeration support computational reasoning. Exercises and projects require students to write, trace, test, debug and explain programs that solve problems of moderate complexity.
evidenceFields.topics: Python language fundamentals; Strings and input/output; Branching and loops; Functions; Tuples, lists, sets and dictionaries; Aliasing and cloning; Recursion; Exceptions and assertions; Object-oriented programming; Inheritance; Computational problem-solving
evidenceFields.methods: Structured programming in Python; Object-oriented programming; Recursive problem-solving; Program tracing; Testing and debugging; Exception handling

courses.name: Introduction to Data Science
courses.contribution: Actual R data cleaning, joining, exploration, visualisation and research-project reporting supply relevant data-analysis methods. No specific animal dataset or full advanced statistical-model curriculum guaranteed.

evidenceFields.description2: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
evidenceFields.profile: Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. Students import, clean, transform and join data, explore patterns, and construct visualizations using tidy-data principles and the grammar of graphics. Web scraping and basic programming functions extend the workflow. A student research project applies these tools to a question using data from a field of interest.
evidenceFields.topics: Data visualization; Exploratory data analysis; Tidy data; Data transformation and integration; Dates and times; Web data; Text data; Geospatial data; Programming functions; Data-based research questions
evidenceFields.methods: R programming; ggplot visualization and grammar of graphics; Data cleaning, tidying and transformation; Data import and joins; Web scraping; Text-data analysis; Geospatial-data analysis

courses.name: Personal & Professional Development
courses.contribution: Required Year1PPD: scholarly research/writing, presentation, reflection, goals and community engagement.

evidenceFields.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
evidenceFields.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
evidenceFields.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
evidenceFields.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design

courses.name: Mathematical Methods
courses.contribution: Functions, calculus, differential equations and actual population-growth/predator–prey modelling directly support quantitative ecology and physiological models. Current detailed content is calculus/dynamics; do not infer a full linear-algebra sequence from the short description.

evidenceFields.description2: Introduces linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues) and calculus (limits, differentiation, integration) to construct and solve equations. Provides problem‑solving skills applicable across disciplines.
evidenceFields.profile: Develops single-variable calculus and related mathematical tools for modelling scientific problems. Functions, limits and differentiation lead to optimization, Taylor series, complex numbers, integration and differential equations. Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica, including numerical approximation. A project implements, analyzes and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and explanation of the computational results.
evidenceFields.topics: Functions and limits; Continuity; Differentiation; Optimization; Taylor series; Complex numbers; Definite and indefinite integrals; Integration techniques; First-order differential equations; Population-growth and predator–prey models; Second-order linear differential equations; Dynamic models
evidenceFields.methods: Analytical differentiation and integration; Taylor approximation; Newton's method; Numerical integration; Euler's method; Analytical solution of differential equations; Computer algebra with Mathematica; Dynamic-model implementation and analysis

courses.name: Neurobiology
courses.contribution: Direct comparative/evolutionary neurobiology, animal behaviour and welfare, enrichment, regulatory behaviour and3Rs ethical appraisal materially connect neural functioning to animal welfare. It does not reproduce the full ethological/Tinbergen practical sequence.

evidenceFields.description2: Examines evolution and complexity of brains. Explores animal cognition, welfare and research ethics and studies how brain regions and rhythms regulate behaviour through interactive assignments.
evidenceFields.profile: Studies nervous systems and behaviour from comparative, evolutionary and physiological perspectives. Brain anatomy and laboratory introductions support analysis of animal behaviour, research models and welfare. The second part connects regulatory behaviour and biological rhythms to sleep, lifestyle drugs, mood and eating disorders. Comparative-anatomy work and a literature-based disorder report apply neurobiological concepts while animal-research assignments examine reduction, refinement and replacement.
evidenceFields.topics: Nervous-system evolution and comparative anatomy; Brain cells and morphology; Cerebral circulation and nerves; Animal behaviour and welfare; Sentience and research ethics; Reduction, refinement and replacement; Enrichment and brain development; Regulatory and sexual behaviour; Lifestyle drugs; Circadian rhythms and sleep; Sleeping and eating disorders; Depression and anxiety; Gut-brain axis; Hypothalamus and pineal gland; Dying brain and consciousness
evidenceFields.methods: Comparative brain-anatomy analysis; Introductory microscopy and cell staining; Brain-model comparison; Ethical appraisal of animal research and the 3Rs; Literature-based analysis of neurobiological disorders

courses.name: Conservation Biology
courses.contribution: Actual habitat loss/fragmentation, overharvesting, endangered-species management and conservation-status analysis support animal-population protection and human impacts. No captive-breeding husbandry or rewilding placement is promised.

evidenceFields.description2: This course explores environmental conservation through biological and social science perspectives. Topics include biodiversity importance, threats to ecosystems, conservation methods, and tools to monitor and protect nature. It also covers national and international laws, policies, and initiatives aimed at preserving ecosystems and ensuring a sustainable future for current and future generations.
evidenceFields.profile: Introduces conservation biology through biodiversity loss, its human causes and possible responses. Students examine habitat destruction and fragmentation, overharvesting, invasive species, climate change, disasters and extinction, followed by conservation planning, species management and conservation in altered landscapes. A local threatened-species project investigates conservation status and protection measures and develops a public-awareness flyer.
evidenceFields.topics: Biodiversity and ecosystems; Anthropogenic extinction; Habitat loss and fragmentation; Overharvesting; Invasive species; Climate impacts; Natural and human-caused disasters; Conservation priorities; Endangered-species management; Human-modified landscapes; People and conservation; Conservation-study design and evaluation
evidenceFields.methods: Threatened-species conservation-status analysis; Assessment of species-protection measures; Evidence-based conservation communication

courses.name: Biochemistry
courses.contribution: Enzymes, carbohydrate/lipid/protein chemistry and energy/nitrogen metabolism materially support the biological basis of nutrient use. Feed formulation/manufacture, animal requirements and broiler/fish trials are not covered.

evidenceFields.description2: Explores the chemistry of life and biomolecules such as proteins, sugars, lipids and nucleic acids. Discusses metabolic pathways, the role of biomolecules in health and disease and applications in medicine, biotechnology and sustainability.
evidenceFields.profile: Examines the chemistry of life, emphasizing biomolecular structure and function, enzymes and metabolic pathways. Students study proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, enzyme kinetics and regulation, glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, the citric-acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation and further carbohydrate, lipid and nitrogen metabolism. Protein-biochemistry techniques are discussed. A literature-based disease project links a biochemical defect to symptoms, diagnostics and treatment, keeping the molecular mechanism central.
evidenceFields.topics: Water and weak bonds; Amino acids and protein structure; Protein-biochemistry techniques; Enzyme action, kinetics, regulation and inhibition; Hemoglobin; Carbohydrates and lipids; Metabolic organization; Glycolysis and gluconeogenesis; Citric-acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation; Glycogen and pentose-phosphate metabolism; Fatty-acid and lipid metabolism; Nitrogen and urea cycle; Biochemical mechanisms of disease
evidenceFields.methods: Biochemical pathway and disease-mechanism analysis; Primary-literature review

courses.name: Epidemiology & Public Health
courses.contribution: Direct disease-frequency/risk measures, study design, bias/confounding, causality and outbreak reasoning contribute population-level health evidence. Human public-health projects do not supply veterinary-economic decision analysis.

evidenceFields.description2:
Public health is about changing the world. From pandemics to lifestyle-related diseases, from screening for disease to improving water and air quality, it asks: how can we improve to keep the population healthy?_x000D_
But how do we know what actually works? In this course you will dive into epidemiology: the science behind public health. You will learn how to study disease, risks, and changes over time, and how to critically evaluate evidence. Because behind every public health decision lies a question of evidence, and by the end of this course, you will be equipped to engage with it. This course invites you to look beyond the lab, the hospital, and the library, into the wider world where health is shaped. What matters most if we truly care about health, and how can we influence that?
evidenceFields.profile: Introduces epidemiological reasoning and its application to public health. Students measure and interpret disease patterns, study research designs, association, bias, confounding and causality, then examine health determinants, promotion, needs assessment and screening. A local project analyzes a Zeeland health challenge, compares population data, considers affected groups and interventions, and incorporates stakeholder perspectives into feasible recommendations.
evidenceFields.topics: Disease frequency and risk; Incidence and prevalence; Measures of association; Epidemiological study designs; Bias, confounding and causality; Outbreak investigation; Social and environmental health determinants; Health inequalities; Health promotion; Health-needs assessment; Screening; Evidence-informed interventions and implementation
evidenceFields.methods: Epidemiological rate and risk calculation; Descriptive and analytic epidemiology; Study-design and evidence appraisal; Population-health data interpretation; Outbreak analysis; Health-needs assessment; Stakeholder interviewing; Evidence-informed intervention development

courses.name: The Science of Evolution
courses.contribution: Population/quantitative genetics, natural selection, adaptation, sexual reproduction, life histories and Tinbergen-based evolutionary analysis directly support animal diversity and evolution. Designing a livestock genetic-improvement programme is an additional specialist skill.

evidenceFields.description2: Evolution is the unifying theory in biology. As such, an understanding of evolutionary biology is vital for understanding the natural world. In this course, we will discuss key concepts in evolution such as population genetics, variation and selection, speciation, macro-evolution and the origins of life. The importance of evolutionary concepts to all other fields of biology will be emphasized, as well as important implications of evolutionary processes in fields like human health and climate change.
evidenceFields.profile: Examines evolutionary theory from genetic mechanisms to the diversification and history of life. Students study natural selection, variation and drift, population and quantitative genetics, adaptation and sexual reproduction, then species concepts, speciation, phylogeny and macroevolution. Genomics, development, biogeography and coevolution extend the account across scales. A project reconstructs a chosen species' evolutionary history using Tinbergen's four questions.
evidenceFields.topics: Evidence for evolution; Molecular and Mendelian genetics; Natural selection and genetic drift; Multilocus and quantitative genetics; Adaptation and units of selection; Sexual reproduction; Species concepts and speciation; Phylogeny and classification; Evolutionary biogeography; Evolutionary genomics and development; Coevolution; Evolutionary rates, extinction and radiation
evidenceFields.methods: Evolutionary-history analysis using Tinbergen's four questions; Phylogenetic reconstruction

courses.name: Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy
courses.contribution: Actual environmental/social/health life-cycle assessment, circular resource use, cost/revenue analysis and product/process appraisal supply substantive sustainability methods for production systems. Animal-food supply chains are applications, not guaranteed course projects.

evidenceFields.description2: Teaches evaluation of environmental impacts of products, processes and services throughout their lifecycle. Emphasises strategic planning for a circular economy through hands‑on learning.
evidenceFields.profile: Develops life-cycle approaches to evaluating products, processes and services within a circular economy. Students examine environmental, social and health consequences from resource extraction to disposal or reuse, together with costs, revenues and management strategies. Three preliminary projects develop different parts or forms of life-cycle analysis, followed by a project that integrates the stages into a full product or process assessment.
evidenceFields.topics: Circular economy; Product and process life cycles; Resource extraction and reuse; Environmental impacts; Social and health consequences; Life-cycle management strategies; Product-based and process-based assessment; Costs and revenues; Sustainable product and process planning
evidenceFields.methods: Life-cycle assessment; Life-cycle management strategy analysis; Environmental-impact estimation; Cost and revenue analysis; Integrated product or process assessment

courses.name: Molecular Cell Biology
courses.contribution: Cell membranes, signalling, trafficking, gene regulation, tissues and bioenergetics are substantial mechanisms of animal cell function; research-method appraisal complements experimental study without claiming this taught course is wet-lab training.

evidenceFields.description2: Provides foundation for practical applications in life science. Focuses on cellular biology of eukaryotes and prokaryotes, revisits concepts from introductory courses, examines current research and encourages evaluating reproducibility and modernising methods.
evidenceFields.profile: Studies the molecular mechanisms underlying cellular structure, physiology and regulation, primarily in eukaryotes. Bioenergetics, proteins and membranes connect to genome replication, repair and gene expression, followed by trafficking, signalling, division, tissues, stem cells and cancer. Students evaluate research methods and reproducibility and investigate a drug's molecular target, therapeutic action, metabolism and adverse effects through primary literature, a paper and a research poster.
evidenceFields.topics: Cellular components and bioenergetics; Proteins and membranes; Cytoskeleton; DNA replication and repair; Genomes; Regulation of gene expression; Membrane transport and trafficking; Cell-signalling pathways; Cell division and fate; Tissue organization; Stem cells; Cancer; Molecular mechanisms of drug action
evidenceFields.methods: Critical analysis of primary molecular-biology literature; Evaluation of research-method limitations and reproducibility; Thermodynamic free-energy calculations; Molecular mechanism analysis

courses.name: Life Science Laboratory
courses.contribution: Actual microbial culture/identification, antibiotic susceptibility, ELISA, protein purification, PCR and DNA analysis provide molecular/host-pathogen experimental tools. No animal-handling internship or live-animal physiology practical inferred.

evidenceFields.description2: Introduces biochemical and molecular laboratory work. Covers themes like blood, proteins, bacteria, DNA and bioinformatics and provides a foundation for clinical and biomedical research.
evidenceFields.profile: Provides hands-on training in biochemical, microbiological and molecular laboratory methods. Blood analysis, microbial culture and hygiene lead into bacterial transformation, green fluorescent protein production and purification, DNA isolation and analysis, and introductory bioinformatics. Students follow and sometimes adapt protocols, interpret experimental results, maintain reproducible laboratory records and communicate findings in scientific reports and figures.
evidenceFields.topics: Blood cells and proteins; Blood groups and hemograms; Aseptic culture and bacterial identification; Disinfection and sterilization; Antibiotic susceptibility; Genetically modified bacteria; GFP production and purification; DNA and plasmid analysis; PCR and restriction digestion; Protein and DNA databases; Genotype and population-genetic interpretation; Experimental reproducibility
evidenceFields.methods: Pipetting and workflow planning; Microscopy and blood-smear examination; Blood cell counting and hemogram measurement; ELISA; Aseptic culture and purity streaking; Bacterial identification and inhibition-zone testing; Sterilization and disinfection testing; pGLO bacterial transformation; Protein extraction and chromatographic purification; SDS-PAGE; DNA and plasmid isolation; PCR; Restriction digestion and agarose-gel electrophoresis; DNA and protein database searching; Laboratory notebook and scientific-report preparation

courses.name: Ecosystems Uncovered: How Nature Works
courses.contribution: Direct conditions/resources, niches, competition, predation, population dynamics and food-web/energy models explain animal–environment relationships. R ecological modelling and a research poster provide actual quantitative inquiry.

evidenceFields.description2: Focuses on basic principles of ecology. Studies how environmental conditions affect organisms and examines ecological principles governing individuals, populations, communities and ecosystems, including ecological modelling and applied case studies.
evidenceFields.profile: Develops ecological principles from organisms and populations to communities and ecosystems. Environmental conditions, resources and life cycles frame competition, feeding relationships, selection, population dynamics and biodiversity. Energy and matter cycles connect ecological processes to conservation and human impacts. Dedicated practical sessions teach simple ecological modelling in R, and a small research project communicates findings through a poster.
evidenceFields.topics: Ecology and evolution; Environmental conditions and resources; Climate and life cycles; Ecological niches; Competition and cohabitation; Predation and food webs; Natural selection; Population dynamics; Biodiversity patterns; Ecological succession; Ecosystem energy and matter fluxes; Global cycles; Conservation and human impacts; Ecosystem value
evidenceFields.methods: Ecological modelling in R; Population-dynamics calculations; Ecosystem energy and matter-flux calculations; Ecological research-project design and analysis

courses.name: Ethics
courses.contribution: Ethical theories, argument reconstruction and independent philosophical judgment directly support dilemmas about responsibility to animals; the course description explicitly includes animal rights. No animal-welfare measurement protocol is invented.

evidenceFields.description2: Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality.
evidenceFields.profile: Studies moral reasoning through historical and contemporary ethical theories and close philosophical reading. Utilitarianism, consequentialism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics lead into Nietzsche's genealogy, Murdoch's account of goodness and Nagel's treatments of value, perspective, death and meaning. Reflection and research essays require interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.
evidenceFields.topics: Divine command and human nature; Moral relativism and universalism; Utilitarianism and consequentialism; Kantian ethics; Virtue ethics; Social contract and intuitionism; Feminist and care ethics; Nietzschean genealogy and nihilism; Murdoch's sovereignty of good; Moral value and perspective; Death, absurdity and meaning; Ethical theory and practical judgment
evidenceFields.methods: Close philosophical text analysis; Reconstruction and critical evaluation of moral arguments; Comparison of ethical theories; Conceptual analysis; Independent philosophical argument development

courses.name: Human Physiology
courses.contribution: Homeostasis, endocrine/nervous regulation, respiration, digestion/metabolism, growth and reproduction give substantial shared mammalian functioning. Actual study is human physiology; species-specific adaptations, husbandry and WUR animal practicals are additional.

evidenceFields.description2: Studies normal functioning of the human body, covering structure‑function relationships, energy handling, homeostasis, signalling, organ systems and integration of their functions.
evidenceFields.profile: Studies normal function and regulation in the adult human body, linking molecular and cellular processes to integrated organ systems. Homeostasis, signalling and energy handling frame nervous, endocrine, muscular, respiratory, cardiovascular, renal, digestive and reproductive functions. Medical examples illustrate physiological principles. An individual literature-based paper examines a selected physiological or pathophysiological process and is developed through structured peer review and revision.
evidenceFields.topics: Cells, tissues and membrane dynamics; Homeostasis and control; Cellular signalling; Endocrine and nervous regulation; Muscles and movement; Breathing and gas exchange; Blood and cardiovascular function; Renal function; Fluid and electrolyte balance; Digestion and metabolism; Growth and exercise physiology; Reproduction and development
evidenceFields.methods: Physiological literature review; Medline/PubMed literature searching; Scientific peer review and evidence-based revision

courses.name: Molecular Pathology & Genetics
courses.contribution: Inheritance, genetic variation, epigenetics, molecular diagnosis and tissue injury/inflammation support biological health/genetics mechanisms and research design. The human disease/genetic-treatment context does not implement livestock breeding-program optimisation.

evidenceFields.description2: Covers general and molecular pathology and genetics. Studies cell injury, death, inflammation, immunity, tissue repair, regeneration, fibrosis and neoplasia, examines genetic mutations and diseases, and discusses genetic testing and ethical considerations.
evidenceFields.profile: Connects cellular pathology with the genetic mechanisms of human disease. Students examine injury and death, inflammation and repair, neoplasia and lymphoid malignancies, then inheritance, genetic variation, epigenetics, molecular diagnosis and genetic treatment. Ethical, legal and safety questions accompany genetic technologies. A two-year research-grant proposal integrates literature, hypotheses, method selection, controls, feasibility and budgeting; an ethics debate examines stakeholder positions.
evidenceFields.topics: Cell injury, adaptation and death; Acute and chronic inflammation; Regeneration, repair and fibrosis; Neoplasia; Pulmonary pathology; Leukemia and lymphoma; Genes, genomes and inheritance; Genetic variation and chromosome abnormalities; Gene regulation and epigenetics; Genotype-phenotype relationships; Genetic testing and DNA technologies; Gene-based therapies and cell manipulation; Genetics ethics, law and biosafety
evidenceFields.methods: Biomedical literature review; Research-grant proposal design; Hypothesis formulation and experimental-control selection; Research feasibility, timeline and budget planning; Stakeholder-based ethical argument analysis

courses.name: Marine Biology
courses.contribution: Actual marine ecosystems, production, food webs, fisheries/aquaculture seminars and human impacts support aquatic-animal ecology. Cultivation-specific feeding, reproduction, energetics and fish-health practicals remain additional.

evidenceFields.description2: Studies ecological processes in marine environments such as estuaries, rocky shores and coral reefs. Examines human impacts and includes guest lectures, lab visits, excursions and field work, culminating in an essay.
evidenceFields.profile: Examines marine ecological processes, ocean systems and human impacts on the sea. Physical and chemical oceanography support the study of primary and secondary production, microbial ecology, and habitats from estuaries and shores to the open ocean, deep sea and polar regions. Student seminars address fisheries, aquaculture, acidification, sea-level rise and plastic pollution. A multimedia outreach project translates a marine biological topic for a public audience.
evidenceFields.topics: Physical and chemical oceanography; Primary and secondary production; Marine microbial ecology; Estuaries; Rocky and sandy shores; Pelagic and continental-shelf ecosystems; Deep-sea ecosystems; Mangroves and seagrass; Coral reefs; Polar marine environments; Fisheries and aquaculture; Ocean acidification and sea-level rise; Marine plastic pollution
evidenceFields.methods: Multimedia marine-science communication

courses.name: Probability & Statistics
courses.contribution: Probability, estimation, confidence intervals, testing and simulation supply rigorous inferential tools for animal/population evidence; does not replace all life-science advanced regression/ANOVA training.

evidenceFields.description2: Provides a foundation in mathematical statistics. Covers probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; uses computer algebra software to develop theoretical understanding and practical skills.
evidenceFields.profile: Provides a rigorous introduction to probability and mathematical statistics, from probability spaces and random variables to multivariate distributions and statistical inference. Students study estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and maximum-likelihood methods, followed by an introduction to Bayesian reasoning. Mathematica simulations verify analytical results. A substantial project implements and compares random-sampling algorithms, including inverse sampling, accept-reject sampling and Gibbs sampling.
evidenceFields.topics: Probability spaces and conditional probability; Random variables and expectation; Moment-generating functions; Discrete and continuous distributions; Multivariate and conditional distributions; Transformations and correlation; Sampling and order statistics; Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests; Estimation efficiency; Bayesian inference; Monte Carlo methods
evidenceFields.methods: Analytical probability calculation; Maximum-likelihood estimation and testing; Chi-square tests; Bootstrap; EM algorithm; Bayesian updating; Inverse-transform sampling; Accept-reject sampling; Gibbs sampling; Monte Carlo simulation in Mathematica

courses.name: Infection & Immunity
courses.contribution: Innate/adaptive immunity, immune evasion, mucosal defence, vaccination and inflammatory pathology give substantial host-defence mechanisms with actual flow-cytometry-data analysis. Animal housing/climate thermoregulation is a distinct missing focus.

evidenceFields.description2: Explores fundamental processes in immunology such as recognition of self vs non‑self, lymphocyte receptor development and innate and adaptive immune responses. Examines host‑pathogen interactions, inflammation, tissue damage and immunopathology.
evidenceFields.profile: Examines host-microbe interactions and the immune mechanisms that protect against infection or cause disease. Microbiology and innate defence lead into antibodies, antigen recognition, lymphocyte development and memory, effector responses and mucosal immunity. Vaccination, allergy, immunodeficiency and autoimmunity connect mechanisms to clinical problems. Students analyze lymphocyte phenotypes using original flow-cytometry data and synthesize recent research in an extended and graphical abstract.
evidenceFields.topics: Infectious agents and microbial virulence; Host defence and immune evasion; Immune cells, organs and cytokines; Innate immunity and complement; Antibodies and antigen recognition; MHC and lymphocyte receptors; Lymphocyte activation, development and memory; Cell- and antibody-mediated immunity; Mucosal immunity; Vaccination and viral infections; Hypersensitivity and allergy; Immunodeficiency; Autoimmune disease; Outbreak management
evidenceFields.methods: Flow-cytometry data analysis and lymphocyte phenotyping; Clinical symptom and mechanism analysis; Medline/PubMed literature searching; Critical analysis of immunological research; Graphical synthesis of scientific findings

courses.name: Mechanisms of Disease
courses.contribution: Human organ-system pathophysiology and mechanistic clinical-case reasoning deepen how dysfunction follows physiology. This is a bounded complementary mechanism contribution, not veterinary diagnosis, farm-animal disease management or the additional inflammation-focused WUR course.

evidenceFields.description2: Examines molecular and cellular defects triggering pathologies. Presents clinical cases, discusses disease mechanisms and treatments across systems and includes an assignment to invent an imaginary disease.
evidenceFields.profile: Connects normal organ function to pathophysiology across digestive, cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, endocrine and nervous systems. Students integrate anatomy and physiology to explain symptoms, disease mechanisms, diagnostic findings, treatment and prognosis. Published clinical cases develop differential reasoning and appraisal of diagnostic procedures. A creative assignment constructs an imaginary disease whose symptoms, mechanism and proposed treatment must form a coherent pathophysiological account.
evidenceFields.topics: Organ-system disease mechanisms; Nutrition and digestive disease; Hematological and cardiovascular disease; Respiratory disease; Renal failure, dialysis and transplantation; Endocrine disorders; Neurological disease; Etiology and pathogenesis; Diagnosis, treatment and prognosis; Medical ethics; Rheumatic disease
evidenceFields.methods: Clinical case analysis; Differential diagnosis reasoning; Critical appraisal of diagnostic and laboratory procedures; Integration of anatomy, physiology and clinical evidence; Mechanistic modelling of an imaginary disease; Biomedical literature comparison

courses.name: Sustainable Farming & Innovation
courses.contribution: Actual animal husbandry, aquaculture, alternative proteins and comparative environmental appraisal of farming/innovation provide a substantial direct sustainable-production contribution. The literature project is not animal-feed manufacture or an animal-care placement.

evidenceFields.description2: Discusses environmental impacts of agriculture and explores sustainable agriculture approaches such as agroecology, organic farming, conservation agriculture, precision agriculture, sustainable livestock farming, agroforestry, permaculture, crop rotation, integrated pest management and sustainable supply chains.
evidenceFields.profile: Examines how food production can balance human needs with environmental impacts. Students assess current agriculture, horticulture and animal husbandry, their effects on biodiversity and ecosystems, and alternative practices and innovations. Aquaculture, alternative animal-protein sources and farming for other industries extend the comparison. A literature-based project critically investigates a chosen sustainable-farming question and reports the evidence without prescribing a single preferred approach.
evidenceFields.topics: Agricultural and horticultural systems; Environmental impacts of farming; Wildlife and biodiversity; Modification of current farming practices; Alternative agricultural approaches; Animal husbandry; Aquaculture; Alternative protein sources; Farming for non-food industries; Sustainable-farming innovation
evidenceFields.methods: Scientific-literature review; Comparative appraisal of farming practices and innovations

courses.name: Governance of Sustainability
courses.contribution: Food governance, institutions, public goods/externalities, stakeholder power and policy evaluation give concrete tools for sustainable animal-production decisions. Actual project is a Zeeland issue, not necessarily livestock.

evidenceFields.description2: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
evidenceFields.profile: Analyzes sustainability as a problem of collective decision-making involving governments, markets and civil society. Concepts of institutions, power, participation, justice and problem complexity frame competing technological and systemic responses. Structured cases examine food, freshwater, energy and climate mitigation. Students apply governance frameworks to a Zeeland issue, consult relevant organizations or experts, and produce policy advice or an evaluation assessing effectiveness, feasibility and stakeholder interests.
evidenceFields.topics: Institutions, actors and power; Collective action and common-pool resources; Governance modes and networks; Techno-optimism and ecological limits; Climate justice; Populism and environmental politics; Wicked and long-term problems; Public participation; Food, water and energy governance; Markets, public goods and externalities; Adaptive and global governance; Climate mitigation; Policy effectiveness and feasibility
evidenceFields.methods: Governance-framework application; Problem diagnosis and causal analysis; Stakeholder and policy-option matrices; Policy evaluation; Policy-advice memo development; Stakeholder and expert interviewing; Comparative analysis of normative policy perspectives

courses.name: Sustainability Essentials I
courses.contribution: Chemical equilibrium, molecular interactions, thermodynamics, energy and physical modelling supply a bounded foundation for physiological/biochemical processes. Actual starch-polymer experiment is materials work, not feed processing or bio-organic stereochemistry.

evidenceFields.description2: Provides key concepts in physics, chemistry, materials science, mathematics and modelling necessary for sustainability. Uses a case study to connect concepts to real‑world sustainability challenges and prepares students for 200‑level sustainability courses.
evidenceFields.profile: Uses planetary boundaries to introduce scientific tools for understanding sustainability and human impacts on Earth systems. Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and learn chemical, thermodynamic and mechanical principles relevant to environmental processes. Topics connect climate, ocean acidification, nutrient cycles, energy and materials. An iterative laboratory project makes starch-based biopolymers and measures their strength and elasticity to improve the formulation.
evidenceFields.topics: Planetary boundaries and the Anthropocene; Exponential growth and environmental change; Graphs, rates and uncertainty; Dynamic systems; Chemical bonds, reactions and equilibria; Ocean acidification and nutrient cycles; Thermodynamics and entropy; Greenhouse gases and energy; Ozone depletion; Newtonian mechanics, stress and strain; Biopolymers and material properties
evidenceFields.methods: Graph interpretation and comparison; Fermi estimation; Difference-equation and first-order linear differential-equation modelling; Elementary differentiation and integration; Biopolymer preparation; Strength and elasticity measurement; Iterative experimental improvement

courses.name: Introduction to Brain & Behavior
courses.contribution: Neural signalling, brain organisation, learning and behavioural/neuroscience evidence appraisal prepare advanced research synthesis and complement comparative neurobiology. Human psychology is not animal husbandry.

evidenceFields.description2: Explores why people behave as they do and how brain injuries affect mental processes. Discusses nature and nurture, introduces brain anatomy and psychological theories, and provides a gateway to cognitive science and clinical psychology.
evidenceFields.profile: Introduces psychological and neuroscientific explanations of behaviour and mental processes. Students study neural signalling, brain anatomy and development, learning, intelligence, personality, social influence, mental disorders and treatments. Several sessions introduce behavioural, imaging and electrophysiological approaches to neuroscience and their combined use. Interdisciplinary research-article and case analysis connects psychological processes to neural mechanisms and clinical questions.
evidenceFields.topics: Brain and behaviour; Neural signalling and action potentials; Functional neuroanatomy; Brain development and hemispheric specialization; Associative, non-associative and social learning; Intelligence; Personality and self-concepts; Social influence; Mental disorders and DSM-5-TR; Psychological treatment; Neuroimaging, electrophysiology and converging methods
evidenceFields.methods: Psychological and neuroscientific research appraisal; Interdisciplinary case-study analysis

courses.name: Statistics & Experimental Methods
courses.contribution: Actual multivariable regression, ANOVA/ANCOVA, categorical/repeated-measures models, diagnostic checks and R analyses provide direct advanced empirical methods for health/biological research.

evidenceFields.description2: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in the medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers in other domains. In addition to technical training, the course emphasizes clear academic communication. It will equip you with the skills necessary to apply advanced statistical techniques to real-world research problems. With a focus on practical application through case studies and data analysis projects, You will be able to choose the appropriate statistical model for various research scenarios and address common challenges in data interpretation.
evidenceFields.profile: Develops experimental-design knowledge and practical statistical analysis for health and behavioural research. Students choose, fit, diagnose and interpret multivariable models, comparing means, analyzing categorical outcomes and studying latent constructs. R, primarily through R Commander, supports repeated practical exercises; SPSS is an optional alternative. Data-analysis papers and a poster connect research questions and hypotheses to appropriate models, assumption checks, substantive interpretation and APA reporting.
evidenceFields.topics: Experimental, nonexperimental and quasi-experimental designs; Statistical inference; Correlation and regression; Model assumptions and diagnostics; Group comparisons; Covariate adjustment; Factorial, repeated-measures and mixed designs; Categorical outcomes; Latent constructs and scale reliability; Effect size and power; Statistical reporting
evidenceFields.methods: R and R Commander data analysis; Multiple linear regression and dummy coding; Regression diagnostics; t-tests and nonparametric alternatives; ANOVA and ANCOVA; Factorial, repeated-measures and mixed-design ANOVA; Logistic regression; Exploratory factor analysis; Principal component analysis; Cronbach's alpha; APA statistical reporting

courses.name: Pharmacology
courses.contribution: Pharmacodynamics/kinetics, antimicrobial action and immune/inflammatory drug mechanisms deepen infection/physiology research. Virtual quantitative experiments are not veterinary prescribing or livestock-treatment training.

evidenceFields.description2: Covers the science of drugs—their origin, composition, kinetics, therapeutic use and toxicity. Discusses drug targets, interactions and kinetics, enabling students to explain therapies in terms of molecular targets and physiological consequences.
evidenceFields.profile: Studies how drugs act at molecular, cellular and whole-body levels and how the body handles them. Pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, metabolism, toxicity and pharmacogenomics provide foundations for rational therapies and drug-target identification. Applications emphasize nervous-system drugs, antimicrobial treatment and inflammatory, immune and airway conditions. Quantitative exercises and virtual experiments model drug responses, while a psychoactive-drug project proposes a testable follow-up experiment.
evidenceFields.topics: Drug discovery and targets; Drug-receptor interactions; Pharmacodynamics; Absorption, distribution, metabolism and elimination; Pharmacokinetics; Antimicrobial therapy; Inflammation and immunopharmacology; Autonomic regulation; Neurotransmission and psychoactive drugs; Pharmacogenomics; Drug toxicity; Access to experimental treatments and evidence; Homeopathy
evidenceFields.methods: Concentration-response modelling; Pharmacokinetic time-concentration and time-response analysis; Pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic parameter calculation; Virtual organ-bath experiments; Hypothesis and experimental-design development

courses.name: Machine Learning
courses.contribution: Regression/classification, validation/resampling and predictor evaluation in R/Python develop analysis of complex biological/health data. A predictive model is not causal inference, and an animal-data project is not guaranteed.

evidenceFields.description2: Covers core machine learning techniques from linear regression to advanced tree‑based methods. Discusses strengths and weaknesses and applies methods to real data from fields like medicine, physics and economics.
evidenceFields.profile: Introduces statistical learning for understanding data and predicting outcomes. Students study regression and classification, model accuracy, resampling, regularization, nonlinear models, trees, support vector machines and unsupervised learning. Practical assignments evaluate methods on real data using R or Python. Projects emphasize informative predictor construction, test-set prediction, appropriate model choice and clear reporting of results and limitations.
evidenceFields.topics: Prediction and model accuracy; Regression and classification; Resampling and validation; Model selection and regularization; High-dimensional data; Nonlinear regression; Tree-based learning; Support vector methods; Dimension reduction; Unsupervised learning; Feature engineering
evidenceFields.methods: Linear and logistic regression; Generative classification; Cross-validation and bootstrap; Subset selection; Ridge regression and LASSO; Splines and generalized additive models; Basic and advanced decision-tree methods; Support vector machines; Principal component analysis; Clustering; Predictive-performance evaluation; R or Python implementation

courses.name: Functional Anatomy
courses.contribution: Human skeletal/organ anatomy, imaging and three-dimensional structure–function reasoning deepen physiological mechanisms. This is a partial mammalian-anatomy relationship; comparative vertebrate development and WUR animal dissection/histology are missing.

evidenceFields.description2: Introduces human body functioning using imaging, surface anatomy and dissection materials. Shows how anatomy serves function and discusses ethical considerations of learning from the dead.
evidenceFields.profile: Studies human anatomical structure in relation to function through regional and body-system blocks. Skeletal, thoracic, cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, reproductive and lower urinary anatomy are developed through spatial reasoning, medical images, anatomical drawing and human-specimen material. Guided practicals and dissection-room observation connect three-dimensional relationships to variation. Historical, ethical and societal questions about human remains, representation and sex accompany the anatomical study; activities are framed as academic learning rather than clinical qualification.
evidenceFields.topics: Anatomical terminology and body planes; Medical imaging; Skeletal system and vertebral column; Thorax and pelvis; Respiratory and cardiovascular systems; Abdominal organs and vascular supply; Reproductive and lower urinary systems; Anatomical variation and intersex presentations; Human remains and dissection ethics; History and representation of the body
evidenceFields.methods: Surface-anatomy observation; Anatomical image interpretation; Scientific anatomical drawing; Three-dimensional anatomical reasoning; Guided study of human skeletal remains and anatomical specimens; Ethical reflection on anatomical practice

courses.name: Advanced Research Methods & Statistics
courses.contribution: Systematic reviews, risk-of-bias appraisal, effect sizes, R meta-analysis and moderator/heterogeneity analysis provide substantial research-synthesis methods. A taught group synthesis is not WUR individual original animal-data thesis work.

evidenceFields.description2: This course guides you through combining results from multiple studies using systematic reviews and meta-analysis a method now essential in psychology, medicine, social science and other disciplines. Want to know what really works? Gain hands-on skills in research synthesis that inform evidence-based policy and practice. You’ll search literature, manage data, and present findings that matter. Learn to calculate effect sizes, synthesize results and assess bias using R.
evidenceFields.profile: Teaches systematic review and meta-analysis for synthesizing evidence in medical, behavioural and related research. Students define review questions, search and select studies, extract and code findings, assess bias and compute effect sizes. Hands-on R work fits fixed- and random-effects models, examines heterogeneity and moderators, conducts meta-regression and investigates publication bias. A group project completes a small meta-analysis and presents its methods and results in a research poster.
evidenceFields.topics: Systematic-review purpose and limitations; Review protocols and scope; Literature searching and inclusion criteria; Data extraction and study coding; Risk of bias; Effect-size types and transformations; Fixed- and random-effects models; Effect heterogeneity; Moderators and subgroup differences; Meta-regression; Publication bias; Research synthesis and reporting
evidenceFields.methods: Systematic literature review; Database searching and study screening; Study-data extraction and coding; Critical risk-of-bias appraisal; R programming and data management; Effect-size calculation and conversion; Fixed- and random-effects meta-analysis; Moderator and subgroup analysis; Meta-regression; Publication-bias analysis; Meta-analytic visualization and reporting

courses.name: Introduction to Economics
courses.contribution: Supply/demand, consumer choice, production/costs and strategic interaction explain real resource and incentive constraints on farming businesses. Macroeconomic content is broader; veterinary economics is not inferred.

evidenceFields.description2: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.
evidenceFields.profile: Introduces microeconomic principles and short-run macroeconomic analysis. The microeconomic component examines supply and demand, strategic interaction, consumer choice, production, costs and competitive markets. The macroeconomic component introduces output, unemployment and inflation, then relates goods and financial markets through the IS-LM model. Students use algebra and graphs to explain economic behaviour and apply models to economic issues.
evidenceFields.topics: Supply and demand; Game theory; Rational consumer choice; Individual and market demand; Production and costs; Perfect competition; Aggregate output; Unemployment and inflation; Goods and financial markets; IS-LM model
evidenceFields.methods: Algebraic and graphical economic analysis; Supply-and-demand analysis; Game-theoretic analysis; IS-LM modelling

courses.name: Research Methods & Statistics
courses.contribution: Measurement, sampling, surveys/experiments, inference/regression and R-based project design/data collection supply empirical methods for management and stakeholder evidence. Animal-specific measurement remains additional.

evidenceFields.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
evidenceFields.profile: Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.
evidenceFields.topics: Scientific inquiry and hypotheses; Operationalization and measurement; Reliability and validity; Survey construction and sampling; Randomized and quasi-experimental designs; Nonexperimental and qualitative research; Descriptive statistics; Sampling distributions and estimation; Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals; Association and regression; Research ethics and anonymous data collection
evidenceFields.methods: Survey design; Probability and nonprobability sampling; Experimental and nonexperimental research design; R and R Commander data analysis; Descriptive statistics and visualization; Scale-reliability analysis; One- and two-sample mean tests; ANOVA; Chi-square tests; Correlation and regression; Empirical data collection and analysis

courses.name: Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations
courses.contribution: Business environments, finance/operations, customer needs and actual business-model/plan development supply concrete enterprise tools for sustainable farming innovation. No food/animal-sector venture or full agricultural business qualification is guaranteed.

evidenceFields.description2: Through experiential learning, students turn their own bold ideas into new ventures. No prior business expertise is required as teams work on a startup project from ideation to final pitch while gaining business and entrepreneurial skills in areas such as design thinking, business model and customer validation. The class fosters creativity and collaboration to drive business and social innovation.
evidenceFields.profile: Introduces entrepreneurship and core business functions through the development of a startup concept. Students use design thinking to discover customer needs, define a problem, generate and prototype solutions, and construct value propositions and business models. Marketing, finance, operations, human resources and funding inform a coherent business plan and investor pitch. Entrepreneurial cases and a startup simulation examine decision-making, early growth and business lifecycles, with attention to societal impact and sustainability.
evidenceFields.topics: Entrepreneurial mindset and pathways; Business environments, ownership and competition; Customer needs; Value propositions; Business models; Marketing and sales; Finance and accounting; Venture funding; Operations and human resources; Competitive positioning; Startup growth and business lifecycles; Sustainability and societal impact
evidenceFields.methods: Design thinking; Customer-needs discovery; Ideation and prototyping; Value Proposition Canvas; Business Model Canvas; Business planning; SWOT and risk assessment; Startup simulation

courses.name: Strategy & Digital Transformation
courses.contribution: The available description supports strategy from vision to implementation, responsible digital transformation and industry-case analysis of business models and social responsibility. These are fully considered management tools; no agriculture-specific case is invented.

evidenceFields.description2: The course explores how companies develop strategies and drive responsible digital transformation amid rapid technology change impacting the economy and society. Students develop a strategic plan, from vision to execution, and identify digital value opportunities. Using industry cases, they gain foresight into digital technologies and their impact on strategy, business models and social responsibilities.

courses.name: Public Economics
courses.contribution: Public goods/externalities, efficiency/equity and model-based public-policy analysis supply direct tools for evaluating environmental costs and collective decisions around farming. The course is broader than agricultural economics.

evidenceFields.description2: Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.
evidenceFields.profile: Examines government intervention through the efficiency and equity effects of public policy. Market failure, public goods and externalities provide foundations for studying public production, collective choice, spending and taxation. Health, education, welfare and social insurance illustrate expenditure and redistribution questions. Students apply economic models, interpret data and graphs, evaluate research and develop a research proposal and paper.
evidenceFields.topics: Role and size of government; Market efficiency and failure; Public goods; Externalities; Efficiency and equity; Public production; Public choice; Public expenditure; Health and education policy; Welfare programs; Social insurance; Taxation and redistribution
evidenceFields.methods: Economic model-based policy analysis; Efficiency and equity assessment; Interpretation of economic data and graphs; Critical evaluation of public-economics research

courses.name: Marketing & Consumer Engagement
courses.contribution: Marketing strategy, consumer psychology, responsible branding and primary/secondary consumer research contribute real tools for adoption and demand in sustainable food/enterprise systems. No animal-product marketing project is guaranteed.

evidenceFields.description2: This course unpacks what drives consumer engagement with brands and how marketers build customer trust responsibly. It introduces key marketing concepts, consumer psychology, AI/technology-driven marketing innovation, and brand and communication strategies. Students will explore real-life case studies, develop a strategic marketing plan and learn how marketers build sustainable brand strategies.
evidenceFields.profile: Connects marketing strategy and consumer psychology to responsible brand development and customer engagement. Students study strategic planning, customer experience, qualitative and quantitative insights, brand identity, digital marketing and behavioural framing. Applied projects analyze a company's strategy and response to disruption, design a brand, and investigate a consumer phenomenon using academic literature and primary and secondary evidence. Customer-journey mapping translates findings into recommendations.
evidenceFields.topics: Strategic marketing planning; Marketing mix; Customer centricity and experience; Consumer journeys; Market research and augmented insights; Brand identity and image; Brand partnerships; Digital and social marketing; Responsible marketing; Consumer psychology; Nudging and framing; Emerging technologies and marketing agility
evidenceFields.methods: Marketing-strategy case analysis; Advertising-campaign analysis; Kapferer brand-identity prism; Brand design; Primary and secondary consumer research; Consumer-journey mapping; Disruption-response planning

courses.name: Market Research
courses.contribution: The available description supports planning/conducting customer research, analysing results and presenting business recommendations. This provides substantive empirical enterprise inquiry; no unlisted method or food-sector placement is assumed.

evidenceFields.description2: See how companies figure out what customers love and what they don’t. You’ll plan and carry out real research, analyze what you find, and share your results. Our course shows you how to gather opinions and turn them into smart business ideas. Ready to turn curiosity into career skills? Perfect for future marketers, analysts, or entrepreneurs.

Evolutionary and human genetic mechanisms do not reproduce designing and optimising livestock/companion-animal breeding programmes.
Marine ecology and aquaculture topics are relevant but do not reproduce aquatic-animal cultivation physiology, feeding/growth/reproduction and practicals.
General human reproductive anatomy/physiology does not reproduce farm/companion-species fertility cycles, management and reproductive technologies.
The additional animal-management/inflammation/metabolic/behavioural disorder sequence remains separate; shared host defence is aligned to Immunology and Thermoregulation.

Shared environmental/social appraisal of animal husbandry, aquaculture, alternative proteins and farming innovations. WUR specifically compares competing livestock-food-system narratives, planetary/human/animal health and feed–food/circularity dilemmas.

Shared sustainability assessment, production-system impacts and circular-resource reasoning. WUR integrates systems/linear-programming and qualitative methods in a livestock case; UCR develops product/process life-cycle assessment.
Shared business-environment analysis, marketing/finance/operations and an integrated business plan. WUR applies planning to a food-supply-chain enterprise; UCR develops a new-venture concept.
